key_terms.meaning: T/J = τ/r = Gθ/L — torque, polar second moment of area, shear stress at radius r, modulus of rigidity and twist per unit length are linked by one relation.
In a circular shaft τ varies linearly with radius: zero at the centre, τmax at the outer surface.

key_terms.term: Polar second moment of area J
key_terms.meaning: J = πd⁴/32 for a solid shaft; J = π(D⁴ − d⁴)/32 for a hollow shaft of outer diameter D and inner diameter d.

key_terms.term: Maximum shear stress in a solid shaft
key_terms.meaning: τmax = 16T/(πd³), with T in N·m and d in m.

key_terms.term: Maximum shear stress in a hollow shaft
key_terms.meaning: τmax = 16TD/(π(D⁴ − d⁴)), and it occurs at the outer surface.
θ = TL/(GJ) radians over a length L of uniform section.
The product GJ; it is the torque needed to produce unit twist per unit length.
GJ/L, the torque required to twist a shaft of length L through one radian.
The shaft is safe in strength only if τmax ≤ τallow, the allowable shear stress of the material.
The shaft is safe in stiffness only if θ/L ≤ the allowable twist per metre (often quoted in degrees per metre).
P = 2πNT/60, with P in watts, T in N·m and N in revolutions per minute.
Shafts joined end to end carry the same torque; their angles of twist add: θ = Σ T Lᵢ/(Gᵢ Jᵢ).
Shafts fixed at both ends and loaded together twist equally; each takes torque in proportion to Gᵢ Jᵢ/Lᵢ.
A shaft of linearly varying diameter; torque is constant along it but stress is highest at the small end.
Te = √(M² + T²); a shaft designed for Te alone in pure torsion has the same maximum shear stress as under M and T together.
Me = ½[M + √(M² + T²)]; designing for Me in pure bending gives the same maximum principal stress.
σ1,2 = σ/2 ± √((σ/2)² + τ²), with σ = 32M/(πd³) and τ = 16T/(πd³).
Helix angle small (under about 10°); axial load mainly twists the wire, and δ = 8WD³n/(Gd⁴).
Helix angle large; the load both twists and bends the wire, so the spring is softer than a close-coiled one of the same size.
C = D/d, the ratio of mean coil diameter to wire diameter; a small C means high curvature stress.
K = (4C − 1)/(4C − 4) + 0.615/C, which corrects the simple shear stress for wire curvature and direct shear: τmax = K·8WD/(πd³).
A stack of graduated cantilever strips clamped at the centre; load is shared, giving σ = 6WL/(nbt²) and δ = 6WL³/(Enbt³).
Progressively shorter plates in a leaf spring that keep bending stress nearly uniform along the length.
Series: same load, 1/k = 1/k₁ + 1/k₂. Parallel: same deflection, k = k₁ + k₂.

takeaways: A circular shaft under torque has shear stress that grows linearly from zero at the centre to a maximum at the surface, so material near the axis does little work.
The torsion equation T/J = τ/r = Gθ/L is one equation with three faces: stress, stiffness and twist; the same problem can be asked from any of them.
Design is a two-gate check: the shaft must pass the stress limit (strength) and the twist-per-metre limit (stiffness), and either gate can decide the diameter.
Power depends on torque times speed, so a shaft at high rpm carries the same power with much less torque and a smaller diameter.
Shafts in series share torque and add twist; shafts in parallel share twist and divide torque in proportion to GJ/L.
A tapered shaft keeps the torque constant but pushes the maximum stress to the small end, and its twist needs a logarithmic-type formula, not θ = TL/(GJ).
Bending and torsion together create a plane-stress state on the surface element, and equivalent torque or equivalent bending moment converts it back into a simple design sum.
A close-coiled spring stores energy almost purely in torsion of its wire, which is why its stiffness is Gd⁴/(8D³n) and it is far softer than a straight bar of the same wire.
A leaf spring spreads bending stress along its length by using graduated plates, giving a compact, damped spring for road vehicles.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to derive the torsion equation from its assumptions, separate the strength check from the stiffness check, and finish a full numerical design of a shaft, helical spring or leaf spring with every quantity carrying units.

bank.q: State the assumptions of the simple theory of torsion for circular shafts and derive the torsion equation T/J = τ/r = Gθ/L. Draw the shear stress distribution across a solid section and across a hollow section.
outline: Plane sections remain plane and circular after twisting
Radial lines stay straight, so shear strain varies linearly with radius
Material is homogeneous, elastic and obeys Hooke's law, so τ = Gγ
Torque equals the moment of the shear force about the axis: T = ∫τ·r dA
Substitute τ = τmax·r/R and identify J = ∫r² dA = πd⁴/32
Combine with the twist relation to get the three-part torsion equation
Sketch: straight line from zero at centre to τmax at surface; hollow shaft has a minimum value at the inner radius, not zero

bank.q: Define torsional rigidity and torsional stiffness. Explain, with the two design conditions, how a shaft that is safe in strength may still be rejected.
outline: Torsional rigidity = GJ; torsional stiffness = GJ/L
Strength condition τmax = Tr/J ≤ τallow
Stiffness condition θ/L = T/(GJ) ≤ allowable twist per metre
Long slender shaft: stress small but twist per metre large, so strength passes and stiffness fails
Short thick shaft: stiffness passes easily but stress may exceed the limit
Practical allowable twist often quoted in degrees per metre; state the unit conversion

bank.q: Describe close-coiled and open-coiled helical springs. Explain why the open-coiled spring is softer, and derive the deflection of a close-coiled spring under axial load W.
outline: Close-coiled: helix angle small (a few degrees), coils nearly in one plane
Open-coiled: helix angle large, load resolved into twist and bending of the wire
Close-coiled: load W acts at mean radius R = D/2, so wire carries torque T = WR and negligible bending
Strain energy U = T²L/(2GJ) with wire length L = 2πRn and J = πd⁴/32
δ = ∂U/∂W gives δ = 8WD³n/(Gd⁴)
Stiffness k = Gd⁴/(8D³n) = Gd/(8C³n), C = D/d
Open-coiled spring has an extra bending term with E, so it deflects more for the same load

bank.q: Explain the construction of a laminated leaf spring. What is the purpose of the graduated leaves and the master leaf? Write the expressions for maximum bending stress and central deflection.
outline: Stack of plates of decreasing length, clamped at the centre by a U-bolt
Master leaf is the longest, carries the eyes for mounting
Graduated leaves shorten progressively so each section has about the same stress
Ideal spring behaves like a plate of uniform strength; bending moment WL at the centre
σ = 6WL/(nbt²) with L the half span, b width, t thickness, n number of leaves
δ = 6WL³/(Enbt³) = σL²/(Et)
Rebound clips, nipping and initial curvature mentioned briefly

bank.q: A solid steel shaft of 60 mm diameter runs at 300 rpm with an allowable shear stress of 60 MPa. Find the torque and the power it can transmit. Then find the power carried by a hollow shaft of the same outside diameter and inner-to-outer diameter ratio 0.6 at the same stress and speed.
outline: T = τallow·πd³/16 for the solid shaft
Substitute d = 0.06 m and τ = 60 × 10⁶ Pa to get about 2.54 kN·m
P = 2πNT/60 with N = 300 rpm gives about 80 kW
Hollow shaft: T = τπ(D⁴ − d⁴)/(16D) with d = 0.6D
Ratio of torque capacities = (1 − 0.6⁴)/(1) compared with solid; state the percentage gain
Comment: same outside diameter, less material, more torque

bank.q: A tapered shaft 1.5 m long has end diameters 80 mm and 40 mm and carries a torque of 1.2 kN·m. Take G = 80 GPa. Find the maximum shear stress, locate where it occurs, and find the angle of twist.
outline: Torque is the same at every section
τ = 16T/(πd³) is largest where d is smallest, that is at the 40 mm end
Compute τmax with d = 0.04 m
Twist for a linear taper: θ = (32TL)/(3πG) × (d₁² + d₁d₂ + d₂²)/(d₁³d₂³)
Substitute d₁ = 0.08 m, d₂ = 0.04 m, L = 1.5 m, G = 80 × 10⁹ Pa
Answer in radians, then convert to degrees
Note that θ = TL/(GJ) with an average J would be wrong here

bank.q: A shaft is subjected to a bending moment of 3 kN·m and a torque of 5 kN·m together. The allowable shear stress is 45 MPa and the allowable tensile stress is 80 MPa. Choose a suitable diameter using the maximum shear stress theory and check it by the maximum principal stress theory.
outline: Equivalent torque Te = √(M² + T²)
Diameter from d³ = 16Te/(πτallow)
Equivalent bending moment Me = ½[M + √(M² + T²)]
Diameter from d³ = 32Me/(πσallow)
Take the larger of the two diameters
Check the resulting maximum principal stress against 80 MPa
State that the shaft also carries an axial shear from bending, but it is zero at the surface point of maximum bending stress

bank.q: Design a close-coiled helical spring of spring index 6 to absorb 500 N with a deflection of 40 mm. Take G = 80 GPa and allowable shear stress 350 MPa. Using the Wahl factor, find the wire diameter, the mean coil diameter and the number of active coils.
outline: C = D/d = 6, so D = 6d
Wahl factor K = (4C − 1)/(4C − 4) + 0.615/C
Stress: τmax = K·8WD/(πd³) = K·8W·6/(πd²) solve for d
Round d to a standard wire size and keep D = 6d
Deflection δ = 8WD³n/(Gd⁴) solve for n
Stiffness k = W/δ = Gd⁴/(8D³n) as a check
State that the ends contribute inactive coils

bank.q: A leaf spring for a light vehicle has a span of 1.0 m, width 60 mm, and 10 leaves each 8 mm thick. It carries a central load of 4 kN. Find the maximum bending stress and the central deflection. Take E = 200 GPa.
outline: Half span L = 0.5 m, width b = 0.06 m, thickness t = 0.008 m, n = 10
σ = 6WL/(nbt²)
Substitute and get the stress in MPa
δ = 6WL³/(Enbt³)
Check with δ = σL²/(Et)
Comment on whether the stress is acceptable for spring steel

bank.q: A shaft ABC of length 2 m is fixed at both ends and carries a torque of 6 kN·m at the junction B, 0.8 m from A. The two portions are of the same material and diameter. Find the reacting torques at A and C and the angle of twist at B.
outline: Shafts in parallel: the twist at B is the same for both portions
T_A·L_A/(GJ) = T_C·L_C/(GJ)
Equilibrium: T_A + T_C = 6 kN·m
Solve the two equations; the shorter portion takes the larger torque
θ_B = T_A L_A/(GJ) with the given d and G
State that the twist is measured from a fixed end and both give the same value

bank.q: A hollow shaft and a solid shaft are made of the same material and have the same mass per metre. Compare the torque they can carry at the same maximum shear stress. Evaluate the result for an inner-to-outer diameter ratio of 0.5 and comment on the practical limits of using very thin hollow shafts.
outline: Same mass per metre means equal cross-sectional area
Solid: A = πd²/4, T_s = τπd³/16
Hollow: A = π(D² − d²)/4, T_h = τπ(D⁴ − d⁴)/(16D)
Express T_h/T_s in terms of the diameter ratio k = d/D
For k = 0.5 the hollow shaft carries roughly 1.3 times the torque
Physics: material near the axis contributes little, so removing it costs little strength
Limits: thin wall buckles and dents, poor fatigue and impact behaviour, difficult joints, larger outside diameter

bank.q: Two shafts of the same material and length are connected (i) end to end and (ii) side by side with both ends fixed. Explain how torque and twist distribute in each case, using a gearbox and a machine-tool spindle as examples.
outline: Series: same torque passes through both, twists add, weaker section governs stress
Effective 1/(GJ) = Σ Lᵢ/(GᵢJᵢ); stiffness drops when a thin section is added
Parallel: same twist, torque divides as G₁J₁/L₁ : G₂J₂/L₂
Stiffer member attracts more torque — a design warning, not an accident
Series example: motor shaft, coupling, gearbox input shaft
Parallel example: a shaft keyed inside a sleeve, or a two-support spindle
Failure of one member in series stops power flow; in parallel the other overloads

bank.q: A pump shaft fails repeatedly at a keyway close to the bearing, although the nominal shear stress from torque alone is well below the allowable value. Diagnose the likely causes and explain how you would redesign the shaft using combined bending and torsion.
outline: Nominal τ = 16T/(πd³) ignores bending from belt pull, misalignment and rotor weight
Surface element then has σ = 32M/(πd³) and τ together: plane stress
Principal stresses σ1,2 = σ/2 ± √((σ/2)² + τ²); maximum shear = √((σ/2)² + τ²)
Keyway gives stress concentration, so use a higher factor on the nominal stress
Fatigue: reversed bending with steady torque needs a fatigue-based allowable stress
Redesign: increase diameter at the keyway, use a larger fillet, splines or a key with rounded ends
Check both strength and twist per metre after resizing

bank.q: Compare a close-coiled helical spring and a laminated leaf spring as suspension elements for a road vehicle, on stiffness, space, stress distribution, damping and failure behaviour. Which would you choose for a two-wheeler and which for a truck? Justify.
outline: Coil spring: stiffness Gd⁴/(8D³n), stress uniform along the wire, compact, no natural damping, fails by fatigue crack and drops load
Leaf spring: stress spread along the graduated plates, also locates the axle and provides interleaf friction damping
Coil spring needs separate links and a damper; leaf spring is heavy but simple
Truck: leaf spring for load capacity, spread of stress and built-in location
Two-wheeler: coil spring with a damper for low unsprung mass and ride comfort
Both checked for strength and for stiffness (ride frequency), not strength alone

glossary.def: The twisting moment of a couple about the axis of a shaft, measured in N·m.
The quantity J = ∫r² dA over the cross-section, equal to πd⁴/32 for a solid circle and π(D⁴ − d⁴)/32 for a hollow circle.
The stress acting parallel to a face of an element; in a shaft it acts on the cross-section in the tangential direction.
The angle, in radians, through which a right angle of an element distorts under shear stress.
G = τ/γ, the shear counterpart of Young's modulus; about 80 GPa for steel.
The rotation of one end of a shaft relative to the other, in radians, given by θ = TL/(GJ).
The product GJ of a shaft section, the resistance of the section to twisting.
Torque per unit angle of twist for a shaft of given length, equal to GJ/L.
The requirement that the maximum shear stress in the shaft does not exceed the allowable shear stress.
The requirement that the twist per unit length does not exceed the value allowed for smooth running of the machine.
Shafts connected end to end so that the same torque passes through each and the total twist is the sum of the parts.
Shafts connected so that they twist by the same amount and share the applied torque in proportion to GJ/L.
A shaft whose diameter changes linearly along its length, so that stress is highest and twist is concentrated near the small end.
Te = √(M² + T²), the torque that alone produces the same maximum shear stress as the bending moment M and torque T acting together.
Me = ½[M + √(M² + T²)], the bending moment that alone produces the same maximum principal stress as M and T together.
A normal stress on a plane where the shear stress is zero; in a shaft under M and T these are σ1 and σ2 in the surface element.
The ratio C = D/d of mean coil diameter to wire diameter.
A factor greater than 1 that raises the simple shear stress in a spring wire to allow for wire curvature and direct shear.
D, the diameter of the circle through the centres of the wire cross-sections, equal to outside diameter minus wire diameter.
A helical spring with a small helix angle, in which the axial load chiefly produces torsion of the wire.
A helical spring with a large helix angle, in which the axial load produces both torsion and bending of the wire.
The angle between the wire centre line and the plane perpendicular to the axis of the spring.
A spring made of a stack of flat graduated strips clamped at the centre, loaded at the ends or at the centre.
The initial curvature given to the leaves of a spring so that they fit together and share load from the start.
The energy stored in a twisted shaft, U = T²L/(2GJ), equal to τmax²/(4G) per unit volume for a solid shaft.
